**IMPORTANT: Write all required HTML files plus shared CSS to /app/ before ending your turn. Do not stop after planning or after reading the references — keep going until every file listed in the Output section is written.**

Replicate the multi-page website design shown in the reference screenshots.

**Input:** `/reference/` contains 15 PNG files — one per (page, viewport) pair — named `{page}.{viewport}.png`:

```
blog.desktop.png  blog.tablet.png  blog.mobile.png
cause-overview.desktop.png  cause-overview.tablet.png  cause-overview.mobile.png
donor-dashboard.desktop.png  donor-dashboard.tablet.png  donor-dashboard.mobile.png
impact.desktop.png  impact.tablet.png  impact.mobile.png
projects.desktop.png  projects.tablet.png  projects.mobile.png
```

The 5 pages share a single design system — same nav, footer, colors, typography, button styles — and each page is expected to adapt responsively across the three viewports below. All screenshots are **full-page** captures (height extends below the fold).

| Viewport tag | Width × Height |
| ------------ | -------------- |
| `desktop`    | 1440 × 900     |
| `tablet`     | 768 × 1024     |
| `mobile`     | 375 × 812      |

**Output:** Save HTML + CSS to `/app/`. The grader will look for:

```
/app/blog.html
/app/cause-overview.html
/app/donor-dashboard.html
/app/impact.html
/app/projects.html
```

You may use a shared CSS file (e.g. `/app/styles.css`) and link to it from each HTML. Anything in `/app/` is fair game; CSS files can be referenced via relative paths.

**How you'll be graded:**
Each of your HTML files will be rendered in headless Chromium at every viewport listed above and compared to the corresponding reference screenshot. Cross-page consistency matters — a broken page meaningfully lowers your overall score, and so does a layout that breaks at tablet or mobile widths.

**Constraints:**
- HTML and CSS only. The grader runs offline, so external resources (CDNs, web fonts, hotlinked images) will not load. Design self-contained output.
- No JavaScript is needed; functionality is out of scope.
- Aim for visual replication across all 5 pages at every graded viewport — layout, typography, colors, spacing, and content.
- Avoid horizontal overflow at any of the graded viewports (1440 / 768 / 375 px) — content cut off at the edges will be penalized.

The grader is a black box. Focus on producing faithful visual replicas.

Quarterly report 22 May 2026 · Cardigan Bay

Three years on, the Cardigan Bay saltmarsh is holding sediment faster than projected.

The seven hectares enclosed in spring 2023 are accreting at 11.4 mm of vertical gain per tidal cycle — well above the conservative forecast we drafted with University of Aberystwyth's coastal lab and reported in the 2024 prospectus.

What surprised the team was the early return of Salicornia europaea across the inner basin. Pages 4–11 of the field log set the data alongside drone transects and a frankly muddy account from the wardens.

Peat re-wetting at Bordan Mire: water table holding within 4 cm of surface for 124 of the past 180 days.

The 2024 hag-rewetting on Bordan, machine-blocked last summer to plug 18 lateral runoff drains, has stabilised — the first sphagnum returnees were logged in mid-April. Page 11 reports the bench against last year's hydrograph.

A foundry log for restoration capital — line by line, hectare by hectare.

Gaelic Ground Foundry stewards donor capital into long-tenure restoration: saltmarsh, peatland, kelp, and broadleaf woodland. Every pound is logged in a public ledger, every hectare measured by an independent monitor.

Read prospectus Download annual report (PDF) Also available · 178 page print edition

02FOUNDRY THESISRead time · 3 min

We finance the slow work of getting landscape back in function. Our genres — saltmarsh, peatland, broadleaf, kelp — have one thing in common: restoration takes a working generation to settle and a working century to fully express. Most philanthropic capital is impatient with that timescale.

So the foundry holds capital in tenure. Donors give once; the foundry stewards across decades. We publish the ledger. The board includes two of our wardens. There is no executive bonus and no marketing department, and we are not trying to grow.

The pages that follow are a working accounting of where the foundry's capital has gone, what it grew or did not, and how we report the difference.

Custodian

Maire Ó Briain

Foundress · Director of stewardship

Working from a converted oyster shed in Galway, with field bases in Aberystwyth and Lochaweside.

Tenure since 2013 · One paid sabbatical in 2021 · Has not flown since 2019.

04WHAT THE FOUNDRY DOESFour-fold
a · Tenure

Land first, narrative second

We take in unrestricted gifts and deploy them on durable land tenure — long leases, restoration covenants, or freehold purchase for the very small slice held in trust.

b · Cohorts

Evidence-set against academia

Every cohort is paired with a partnered university lab. Forecast bands are published before planting; year-three results are mapped against them.

c · Hands

Local hands, local payroll

Eleven wardens, two ecologists, and a treasurer are on year-round salary. We don't subcontract critical labour because labour writes the data.

d · Reporting

No greenwashing instruments

No credit issuance, no NFTs, no "rewards." Public ledger, signed independent audit, and the print prospectus you can hold in your hand.
